# A deterministic centerpoint from identical reflected fibers

## Proposition

Let C⊂R^n×R^d be a convex body with nonempty mixed-integer intersection
S=C∩(Z^n×R^d), and let K_z={x:(z,x)∈C}. Assume

    K_(−z)=K_z       for every z∈Z^n.                         (1)

Empty fibers are included in this equality. Write q=dim_H(S),
M=H_q(S), and m_0=H_q({0}×K_0). Then there is a single deterministic
point y∈K_0 such that every closed ambient halfspace H containing (0,y)
satisfies

    H_q(S∩H) ≥ (M+m_0)/[2(q+1)].                              (2)

In particular the normalized depth is at least

    (1+m_0/M)/[2(q+1)].                                      (3)

This is a restricted symmetry theorem, not the general OC conclusion.
The symmetry concerns only the integer coordinates: the continuous fibers
need not be centrally symmetric, have a common centroid, or be homothetic.

## 1. Common intrinsic space and the weighted marginal

For every x∈K_z, assumption (1) gives x∈K_(−z). Convexity of C then yields
(0,x) as their midpoint, so

    K_z⊂K_0       for every integer z.                        (4)

In particular K_0 is nonempty. Since the bounded source has finitely many
integer fibers, its Hausdorff dimension equals their largest affine
dimension. Inclusion (4), together with the presence of the zero fiber,
shows that this dimension is exactly dim(K_0)=q.

Let A=aff(K_0), with its Euclidean q-dimensional Hausdorff measure.
For each z define the finite measure μ_z=H_q restricted to K_z on A.
Fibers of dimension less than q have zero such measure. The maps
x↦(z,x) are isometries, so the disjoint finite fiber decomposition gives

    ν=Σ_z μ_z,     ν(A)=M,     μ_0(A)=m_0>0.                  (5)

Both M and m_0 are finite; positivity of m_0 follows from the relative
interior of the q-dimensional convex body K_0 (and from counting measure
when q=0). Define the weighted marginal

    η=ν+μ_0,       η(A)=M+m_0.                               (6)

Its compact convex support is contained in K_0. The central fiber is
counted twice in η, which is essential to the precise constant below.

## 2. A deterministic ordinary centerpoint, with closed boundaries

We recall the standard finite-measure centerpoint construction and its
proof using finite Helly's theorem. If q=0, A is a singleton and choose
its unique point. Suppose q≥1 and put T=η(A).

Intersect K_0 with all closed halfspaces J of the affine space A having
η(J)>qT/(q+1). Every q+1 of these halfspaces have a common point in K_0:
the union of their complements has measure strictly less than T. The
same assertion holds for q+1 sets that include K_0, using at most q such
complements. Finite Helly's theorem in dimension q therefore gives the
finite intersection property. Compactness of K_0 implies that the full
intersection B is nonempty and compact.

Every y∈B belongs to K_0 and satisfies

    η(G)≥T/(q+1)                                             (7)

for every closed halfspace G of A containing y. Indeed, if η(G) were
smaller, its open complement would have measure greater than qT/(q+1).
That open complement is an increasing union of parallel closed
halfspaces strictly separated from G. By continuity of a finite measure
from below, one of them would have measure greater than qT/(q+1), hence
would occur in the defining intersection B while excluding y. This is a
contradiction. This argument does not discard boundary mass.

To specify one deterministic point, fix an orthonormal coordinate system
on A and successively minimize its q coordinates on B. Each minimization
preserves a nonempty compact set, and after q steps exactly one point
remains. Choose that point y. For q=0, (7) holds with T itself.

## 3. Every shared integer tilt is controlled

It suffices to consider a closed halfspace whose boundary passes through
(0,y): a general containing halfspace contains its parallel through-point
halfspace. Write the latter as

    H={ (z,x): β·z+u·(x−y)≥0 },                              (8)

where (β,u)≠0. Let G={x∈A:u·(x−y)≥0}; if u vanishes on the direction
space of A, this is all of A and (7) still applies. For a nonzero
integer base z define the nonincreasing tail function

    F_z(t)=μ_z({x:u·(x−y)≥t}).

The two identical fibers at z and −z contribute to H the amount

    F_z(−β·z)+F_z(β·z) ≥ F_z(0),                             (9)

because at least one of the two thresholds is nonpositive. This uses
only monotonicity of closed tails and remains valid with boundary mass.
Partition all nonzero bases into unordered pairs {z,−z}. The central
fiber contributes μ_0(G), while (9) yields

    H_q(S∩H)
      ≥ μ_0(G)+Σ_{unordered pairs {z,−z}} μ_z(G)
      = [ν(G)+μ_0(G)]/2
      = η(G)/2
      ≥ (M+m_0)/[2(q+1)],                                   (10)

by (7). This proves (2), including every oblique normal and every closed
containing halfspace. The point (0,y) lies in S itself by construction. ∎

## 4. Exact scope relative to OC

The proposition implies OC for a source satisfying (1) whenever

    2^(n−1)(1+m_0/M) ≥ (q+1)γ_d.                             (11)

In particular, in the full-dimensional continuous case q=d it suffices
that 2^(n−1)≥(d+1)γ_d. Thus for d=2 it proves OC for every such
reflected-fiber source with n≥2. For n=1,d=2 it also suffices that
m_0/M≥1/3. These are explicit regimes of a restricted theorem.

For the n=6,d=2 cube-radius source in
`candidate 7595f089ada4c0aa`, the peak
centroid fails the OC bound, but (3) supplies a different deterministic
point at the same integer base. Its certified normalized depth is at least

    (1+9/737)/6 = 373/2211.

The proof makes no invalid inference that the weighted marginal η has
ordinary depth γ_d. The ordinary centerpoint constant 1/(q+1), together
with the exact pair inequality (9), is sufficient for this conclusion.
